Text | Fanyu Meng

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Fundamentals of Acoustics, the standard Chinese textbook, defines sound intensity as follows:

The time-averaged flow of sound energy through a unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation, also called the mean sound energy flux density.

In everyday acoustic testing we mostly measure sound pressure with a microphone. So why do we need sound intensity at all? That is today’s topic.

1. Why bother?

Why isn’t sound pressure enough to fully describe a source and its sound field? In short, because sound pressure has its limits, and many problems have to be approached in terms of energy and power.

A source radiates energy, and the rate at which it does so is its sound power. Sound power is therefore the most reliable way to characterize a source. A sound pressure reading, by contrast, depends on the environment the source sits in, so it cannot describe the source itself accurately. On top of that, the absorption of acoustic materials is worked out from sound power, and sound insulation is defined as the difference between incident and transmitted sound power. Measuring intensity therefore matters just as much as measuring pressure. Intensity really started to get attention, and to reach a wider audience, once sound power determination by intensity was written into international standards and several countries passed laws setting sound power limits for products.

Intensity measurement is still not a fully mature technique, though. It is not like sound pressure, where you pick up a sound level meter and read off the result: it takes a certain amount of expertise. Our understanding of intensity is also not complete. Active and reactive intensity, for example, have received very little research attention (there isn’t even an official Chinese translation for these two terms yet).

2. Some definitions

Instantaneous sound intensity:

It is the product of sound pressure and particle velocity. Particle velocity is a vector, so intensity is a vector too. For more on particle velocity, see my earlier article:

Particle velocity: there is more to sound than sound pressure

The beauty of this formula is that it is unaffected by steady sources outside the surface, and the surface can have any shape, a box or a hemisphere, for instance. Suppose there is a source outside, and its sound enters the box through the left face. Unless there is an acoustic black hole inside, the same sound leaves through the right face. Back to the formula: because is perpendicular to each face and points outward, the energy from the outside source cancels in the integral. That is why the method is immune to steady external sources.

We are usually more interested in the time-averaged intensity. If we further assume a plane wave, or a monopole in a free field, and look only at the normal component, the intensity becomes

In that case intensity can be obtained directly from sound pressure. Reality is less obliging. We rarely get to study such a tidy source. Take a washing machine: several coupled sources plus the structure of the machine itself make its radiation very complicated. So besides pressure, we have to knuckle down and measure particle velocity as well, to calculate intensity more accurately.

3. Active versus reactive intensity

Now let’s move to the frequency domain. Keeping the same simple assumptions, the active intensity (when people say “intensity” they usually mean active intensity) can be written as

So why invent reactive intensity on top of that?

For a plane wave, pressure and particle velocity are in phase. The same holds in the far field of a point source in free space. In the near field of a point source, however, the two quantities drift partly out of phase. You can see this from the expressions for pressure and particle velocity:

In the far field, r is large and the second term in the brackets is small, so . In the near field, r is small and the second term grows. Because of the imaginary unit j, u and p acquire a phase difference, and the smaller r is, the larger that difference becomes.

To describe this, we introduce two concepts: the active sound field and the reactive sound field. Close to the source the reactive field dominates; farther away the active field takes over.

The reactive intensity of the reactive field describes energy that oscillates back and forth rather than propagating away. It is the imaginary part of :

Reactive intensity was not proposed until the middle of the last century, perhaps because it has no obvious physical meaning of its own. Yet in the near field of a source it is a quantity that describes the sound field conditions precisely. That point comes from Jacobsen’s book, and here it is in his own words:

...quite convenient that we have a quantity that makes it possible to describe and quantify the particular sound field conditions in the near field of sources in a precise manner.

Some studies have also linked reactive intensity to structural vibration. Part of the energy of a vibrating structure is not radiated efficiently. It stays near the source as evanescent waves, oscillating in place, and this is related to the reactive intensity. Because of this, reactive intensity can be used to detect and locate vibration.

Figure 6.1 shows sound pressure and particle velocity measured 30 cm from a small monopole source. Their amplitudes and phases are almost identical. The instantaneous intensity is positive, and in the third panel the reactive intensity is barely visible. This is an active sound field.

Now move the measurement point close to the source. Pressure and particle velocity are nearly in quadrature (90° apart in phase). Multiply them, as the definition says, and the intensity oscillates around zero: energy sloshes back and forth without traveling outward. This is a strongly reactive sound field, and in the third panel the dashed line dominates.

Finally, put the source in a reverberation chamber and measure a few meters away. Pressure and particle velocity are no longer correlated, and the field is neither active nor reactive. It is a diffuse, reverberant field.
